title: The deadly look-alikes
teaches: Camas and death camas, and poison hemlock, water hemlock and Queen Anne's lace: how botanists tell them apart, and why this course gives no advice on eating wild plants

blocks.text: Walk along a roadside ditch in western Washington in early summer and you may pass three plants with tall stems and flat white umbrellas of tiny flowers. All three are in the carrot family (lesson K3). One is Queen Anne's lace, the wild ancestor of the garden carrot. One is poison hemlock, a European weed now common on roadsides, which killed Socrates in Athens in 399 BC.[^socrates] The third, growing where the ground is wet, is water hemlock, often called the most poisonous plant in North America: a small amount of its root can kill an adult by causing violent seizures.

The carrot family is full of food (carrot, parsnip, celery, parsley, dill, fennel) and of some of the deadliest plants there are. Their flowers are nearly the same. It is the rest of the plant that tells them apart.

blocks.caption: Camas and death camas, and three plants of the carrot family. Drawn simply.

blocks.text: Queen Anne's lace has a hairy stem, finely cut leaves, a smell of carrot, and often a single dark purple floret (one tiny flower) in the middle of the white umbrella. Poison hemlock's stem is smooth, often taller than a person, and blotched with purple; botanists describe its smell as musty, like mice. Its sap can be absorbed through skin or a cut, and children have been poisoned using its hollow stems as whistles or peashooters. Water hemlock grows with its feet in water, along ditches, marshes and stream banks. Botanists who have cut one open describe a swollen stem base divided into a row of hollow chambers, oozing a yellowish, poisonous liquid; that is a fact for a field guide, not a test to try. All three vary, and young plants without flowers are much harder to tell apart than the drawings suggest.

On the prairies of Whidbey Island and around the south end of Puget Sound, common camas turns whole meadows blue in May. Its bulbs[^bulb], slow-roasted in pits until sweet, were a staple food of the Coast Salish, the Native peoples of the Puget Sound region, and of peoples across the Northwest. Families tended their camas meadows with fire and digging for generations. Growing in the same meadows is death camas, whose bulb looks almost the same and contains a poison that slows and stops the heart. Ranchers lose sheep and cattle to it, and people have died after mistaking it for camas or wild onion.

In flower they are easy to tell apart: camas has blue to violet stars a few centimetres across, death camas a dense spike of many small cream-coloured flowers. Out of flower, the grass-like leaves and the bulbs are nearly identical. The peoples who tended camas meadows managed that danger with knowledge built up over generations and passed on in person, by people who knew each meadow, every year.[^camas-weeding] A reader of a book has none of that.

parts.title: Why this course gives no foraging advice

blocks.text: Every feature in this lesson varies: hemlock stems are not always spotted, Queen Anne's lace is not always hairy, and a camas meadow can hold white-flowered camas. Most poisonings come from someone who was sure. A drawing, a photograph, a key or a phone app is a good way to learn what to look for and a poor way to decide what to eat, and the mistake can't be undone. This course teaches you to recognise these plants so that you leave them alone. If you want to gather wild food, learn in person from an experienced local forager, one plant at a time, and still don't eat anything you are not certain of.
The carrot family has one more hazard: the sap of giant hogweed, and to a lesser degree of wild parsnip, makes skin burn and blister in sunlight. With all of these plants, look and don't touch.

blocks.caption: Five questions on look-alikes
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which family holds Queen Anne's lace, poison hemlock and water hemlock?
items.why: All three carry tiny flowers in umbrellas, the carrot family's signature, along with carrots, parsley and dill.

items.ask: Which of these marks poison hemlock rather than Queen Anne's lace?
choices: A smooth stem blotched with purple
A single dark floret in the centre of the umbrella
items.why: Queen Anne's lace has a hairy stem and often a dark central floret. Poison hemlock's stem is smooth and often purple-blotched.

items.ask: Why is death camas so easily mixed up with camas?
choices: Out of flower, their leaves and bulbs look nearly the same
Death camas has a sweeter smell
Both grow only where the other does
items.why: In flower, camas is blue and death camas cream. Out of flower, the parts a person would dig are almost the same.

items.ask: Where would you expect water hemlock?
choices: With its feet in water, in ditches and marshes
items.why: Water hemlock grows in wet ground. Its chambered stem base and yellowish sap are among its marks.

items.ask: You are fairly sure a wild plant is Queen Anne's lace. What does this lesson advise?
choices: Don't eat it; fairly sure isn't enough with the carrot family
Check it with a phone app; then it is safe
Check that its stem is hairy; then it is safe
items.why: Most poisonings come from someone who was sure. The course teaches recognition so you leave these plants alone.

summary: **Three white umbrellas, one family.** Queen Anne's lace, poison hemlock and water hemlock are all in the carrot family.
**Water hemlock is often called the most poisonous plant in North America.** It grows in wet ground.
**Stems and smell tell them apart.** Hairy and carroty for Queen Anne's lace; smooth, purple-blotched and musty for poison hemlock.
**Camas and death camas grow together.** Blue stars against a spike of cream flowers; out of flower, nearly identical.
**Telling them apart safely takes knowledge passed on in person.** Native peoples tended camas meadows that way for generations.
**This course gives no foraging advice.** Learn to recognise these plants so you leave them alone.

socrates.title: Socrates and the cup of hemlock
socrates.text: In the *Phaedo*, Plato describes Socrates's death after drinking a cup of crushed hemlock: a numbness and chill rose from his feet up his legs toward his chest, while his mind stayed clear until his breathing stopped. That matches coniine, the poison in *Conium maculatum*, which paralyses the muscles one by one, ending with the diaphragm.

bulb.title: Bulb
bulb.text: A **bulb** is a short underground stem wrapped in thick, fleshy leaves full of stored food, like an onion or a tulip bulb. The plant lives through the dry summer or cold winter on that store and sends up new leaves from the centre.

camas-weeding.title: Keeping death camas out of the harvest
camas-weeding.text: Coast Salish and other Northwest harvesters did not wait until digging time to tell the bulbs apart. Families visited their meadows in spring while the plants were in flower, pulling up the cream-flowered death camas or marking the blue camas, and dug the bulbs later once the seed pods had ripened.
